The bleak reading of Frantz Fanon is also the most testable one. Jansen and Osterhammel characterise Fanon  as "the most influential anticolonial thinker of his time". For more than five decades, the life and works of Fanon have inspired national liberation movements and other freedom and political movements in Sri Lanka, South Africa, and the United States.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Frantz Fanon. Fanon formulated a model for community psychology, believing that many mental health patients would have an improved prognosis if they were integrated into their family and community instead of being treated with institutionalized care. He also helped found the field of institutional psychotherapy while working at Saint-Alban under François Tosquelles and Jean Oury.

The self that experiences Frantz Fanon is a committee, not a king. Frantz Omar Fanon was born on 20 July 1925 in Fort-de-France, Martinique, which was then part of the French colonial empire, into a middle class family. Fanon's mother, Eléanore Médélice, who was of Afro-Caribbean and Alsatian descent, was a shopkeeper.

Reproduction explains more of Frantz Fanon than any philosophy dares to admit. Fanon was the third of four sons in a family of eight children. Two of his siblings died young, including Fanon's sister Gabrielle, with whom he was very close.

Once you see Frantz Fanon as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. The young Frantz Fanon was an avid football player, and played the sport in Martinique, later organizing football matches for patients and staff while working at the Blida-Joinville psychiatric hospital in Algeria. In June 1940, the German victory in the Battle of France resulted in the French Third Republic capitulating to Nazi Germany.

The story Frantz Fanon tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. Martinique came under the control of French Navy elements under Admiral Georges Robert, who were loyal to the collaborationist Vichy regime in France. The war disrupted imports from Metropolitan France to Martinique, leading to major shortages on the island, while Robert's authoritarian regime repressed Martinican Allied sympathizers, hundreds of whom escaped to nearby Caribbean islands.

Meaning is not found in Frantz Fanon — it is manufactured for it. Fanon later described the pro-Vichy regime in Martinique as taking off their masks and behaving like "authentic racists". In January 1943, he fled Martinique during the wedding of one of his brothers, and travelled to the British colony of Dominica in order to link up with other Allied sympathizers.

The cold light on Frantz Fanon leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. Following the uprising, Fanon "enthusiastically" returned to Martinique, where the pro-Allied Free French leader Charles de Gaulle had appointed Henri Tourtet as the colony's new governor. Tourtet raised the 5th Antillean Marching Battalion to serve in Free French Forces (FFL), and Fanon quickly enlisted in the unit at Fort-de-France.

Frantz Fanon did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. After Fanon arrived in Casablanca, he was shocked to discover the extent of racial discrimination in the FFL. Fanon was transferred to a Free French military base in Béjaïa, Algeria, where he witnessed firsthand the antisemitism and Islamophobia of the pieds-noirs, many of whom had supported racist laws promulgated by the Vichy regime.

The honest version of Frantz Fanon starts by giving up the comforting part. In August 1944, Fanon embarked on another troopship at Oran to participate in Operation Dragoon, the Allied invasion of German-occupied Provence. After the American VI Corps secured a beachhead, Fanon's unit came ashore at Saint-Tropez and advanced inland.

Strip Frantz Fanon of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. In Doubs, he participated in several engagements near Montbéliard and was seriously wounded by shrapnel, which resulted in him being hospitalized for two months. Fanon was awarded a Croix de Guerre by Colonel Raoul Salan for his military service.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Frantz Fanon shows exactly where that breaks. In early 1945, he rejoined his unit and fought in the Battle of Alsace. Fanon was transferred to Normandy to await repatriation to the West Indies.

What looks like free choice in Frantz Fanon is older than choice itself. Although Fanon had been initially eager to participate in the Allied war effort, the racism he witnessed during the war disillusioned him. During this time, he campaigned for Aimé Césaire - one of the founders of Négritude and a teacher at the Lycée - who was running to become Martinique's deputy to the first National Assembly of the French Fourth Republic.

Nobody designed the part of Frantz Fanon you experience — it was inherited. Though Césaire never taught Fanon directly, his writings had a profound impact on Fanon's thought. Staying in Martinique long enough to finish his baccalauréat, Fanon returned to Metropolitan France in 1946 to study medicine.

Every serious account of Frantz Fanon eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. Fanon was educated at the University of Lyon, where he also studied literature, drama, and philosophy, sometimes attending Merleau-Ponty's lectures. After qualifying as a psychiatrist in 1951, Fanon did a residency in psychiatry at Saint-Alban-sur-Limagnole under the radical Catalan psychiatrist François Tosquelles, who invigorated Fanon's thinking by emphasizing the role of culture in psychopathology.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Frantz Fanon — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. In 1948, Fanon started a relationship with Michèle Weyer, a white medical student, who soon became pregnant. At his friends' urging, he later recognized his daughter, Mireille, although he had no contact with her.

The selfish-gene reading of Frantz Fanon makes it less romantic and far more precise. Paulin Joachim, who knew Fanon, said that on a number of occasions he had seen Fanon hit Josie. In Lyon, while completing his residency, Fanon wrote and published his first book, Black Skin, White Masks (1952), an analysis of the negative psychological effects of colonial subjugation upon black people.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. Originally, the manuscript was a doctoral dissertation, submitted at Lyon, entitled Essay on the Disalienation of the Black, which was a response to the racism that Fanon experienced while studying psychiatry and medicine at the University in Lyon. The rejection of the dissertation prompted Fanon to publish it as a book.

The feeling that Frantz Fanon means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. Left-wing philosopher Francis Jeanson, leader of the pro-Algerian independence Jeanson network, read Fanon's manuscript and, as a senior book editor at Éditions du Seuil in Paris, gave the book its new title and wrote its epilogue. After receiving Fanon's manuscript at Seuil, Jeanson invited him to an editorial meeting.

Nothing in Frantz Fanon was built for you — it was built for reproduction. Amid Jeanson's praise of the book, Fanon exclaimed: "Not bad for a nigger, is it?" Insulted, Jeanson dismissed Fanon from his office. Later, Jeanson learned that his response had earned him the writer's lifelong respect, and Fanon acceded to Jeanson's suggestion that the book be entitled Black Skin, White Masks.

The psychology underneath Frantz Fanon is simpler and older than the story on top. In the book, Fanon described the unfair treatment of black people in France and how they were disapproved of by white people. Frantz argued that racism and dehumanization directed toward black people caused feelings of inferiority among black people.

Behind Frantz Fanon sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. This dehumanization prevented black people from fully assimilating into white society and into full personhood. This caused psychological strife among black people, as even if they spoke French, obtained an education, and followed social customs associated with white people, they would still never be regarded as French or a Man.

The nihilist does not deny Frantz Fanon — he only refuses to flatter it. After his residency, Fanon practiced psychiatry at Pontorson, near Mont Saint-Michel, for another year and then from 1953, in Algeria. Fanon's methods of treatment started evolving, particularly by beginning sociotherapy to connect with his patients' cultural backgrounds.

What culture calls destiny in Frantz Fanon is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. Following the outbreak of the Algerian revolution in November 1954, Fanon joined the Front de Libération Nationale (FLN), after having made contact with Pierre Chaulet at Blida in 1955. Working at a French hospital in Algeria, Fanon became responsible for treating the psychological distress of the French soldiers and officers who carried out torture in order to suppress anti-colonial resistance.

The genes do not care about Frantz Fanon; they care about copies. Fanon made extensive trips across Algeria, mainly in the Kabylia region, to study the cultural and psychological life of Algerians. These trips were also a means of conducting clandestine activities, notably during his visits to the ski resort of Chrea, which hid an FLN base.

Take away the meaning and Frantz Fanon still functions — that is the disturbing part. By summer 1956, Fanon realized he could no longer support French efforts, even indirectly, through his hospital work. In November, he submitted his "Letter of Resignation to the Resident Minister", which later became an influential text of its own in anti-colonialist circles.

The decision I have reached is that I cannot continue to bear a responsibility at no matter what cost, on the false pretext that there is nothing else to be done.
